add_eyes.name: Emanuel Ringelblum
add_eyes.role: Historian and social-welfare organiser with the Joint Distribution Committee; founder and director of the Warsaw ghetto's secret archive, Oyneg Shabes; aged 39–43
add_eyes.where: Warsaw ghetto, then from February 1943 the 'Krysia' bunker at 79 Grójecka Street on the 'Aryan side'
add_eyes.vantage_label: historian of the ghetto, documenting from inside
add_eyes.authenticity: Working notes kept on loose sheets from September/October 1939 to January 1943, some surviving only as typed copies, some undated, some disguised as private letters. Buried with the Oyneg Shabes archive; the first two caches were recovered in Warsaw on 18 September 1946 and 1 December 1950, the third never found. Earlier English selection: Notes from the Warsaw Ghetto (1958), which was cut and altered; complete critical edition: Ringelblum Archive vol. 29 (Jewish Historical Institute, 2018). The archive is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
add_eyes.bio: Ringelblum began a chronicle for himself in the autumn of 1939 and turned it into a collective project: several dozen teachers, writers and young activists, meeting on the Sabbath, gathered essays, diaries, posters, reports and testimony about what was being done to Polish Jews. In 1942 the group compiled some of the first reports on the killings at Chełmno, which reached London. He escaped the ghetto with his wife and son, was discovered in hiding on 7 March 1944 and was shot with his family and the Poles who had sheltered them a few days later.

sources.title: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia: The Oneg Shabbat Archive
Jewish Historical Institute: Ringelblum's writings in the complete edition of the Archive
IPN: 'Animated by one spirit': Emanuel Ringelblum and the underground archive (PDF)

add_eyes.name: Vasily Grossman
add_eyes.role: Novelist serving as a special correspondent of the Red Army newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star) from August 1941; aged 36–40
add_eyes.where: With the 62nd Army and the 308th Rifle Division in Stalingrad (autumn 1942); in Poland with the advancing front (1944); in Berlin (April–May 1945)
add_eyes.authenticity: Field notebooks kept from 5 August 1941 to May 1945, held by his family and in Russian archives. English selection A Writer at War (ed. and trans. Antony Beevor and Luba Vinogradova, 2005), which interleaves notebook material with his published articles and letters, with editorial linking text; not all passages carry an exact day. Not disputed.
add_eyes.bio: Grossman's notebooks hold what Red Star could not print: the fear, drunkenness and cruelty as well as the courage. His mother was among the Jews murdered in his home town of Berdichev in September 1941, and he became one of the first writers to describe the extermination camps; his 1944 essay 'The Hell of Treblinka' was later used at Nuremberg. The notebooks fed his novels Stalingrad and Life and Fate.

sources.title: HistoryNet: excerpt from A Writer at War on the defence of Stalingrad
National Library of Israel blog: From Treblinka to Stalingrad

add_eyes.name: Leslie Skinner
add_eyes.role: Methodist padre (Royal Army Chaplains' Department) attached to the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry, an armoured regiment
add_eyes.where: Gold Beach, landing near Asnelles (Le Hamel), then the Normandy bocage
add_eyes.authenticity: Pocket diary kept through the Normandy campaign and given to the Imperial War Museums. Entries are short and timed. Published privately as The Man Who Worked on Sundays. Not disputed.
add_eyes.bio: Skinner landed with the first tanks of his regiment and spent the following weeks burying the dead, often under fire and often alone, and writing to their families. His diary is spare, a record of times, places and names rather than reflection, which makes the few personal lines hit hard.

sources.title: History News Network: D-Day through the diary of a padre

add_eyes.name: Douglas J. Raymond
add_eyes.role: Acting petty officer, Royal Canadian Navy, in the destroyer HMCS Saskatchewan; aged 22
add_eyes.where: Off the Normandy coast, screening the invasion fleet against submarines and surface raiders
add_eyes.authenticity: Small diary covering 4–24 June 1944, held by the Library of Virginia (Accession 50043). Not disputed.
add_eyes.bio: Raymond's destroyer guarded the landing forces rather than carrying them, so his D-Day is seen from the sea: smoke, bombardment, and an ocean full of landing craft. That night his flotilla fought German destroyers. He later settled in the United States, which is why his diary sits in a Virginia archive.

sources.title: Library of Virginia, Uncommonwealth: a Canadian sailor's D-Day diary

add_eyes.name: David Samoilov (David Kaufman)
add_eyes.role: Moscow literature student turned Red Army private and reconnaissance clerk; later a leading Soviet poet; aged 24
add_eyes.where: With his unit north-east of Berlin at the war's end
add_eyes.authenticity: Diaries kept from youth to old age, published posthumously as Podyonnye zapisi (Day-by-Day Notes, 2002). Some wartime entries were filled out later. Quoted in Russian anthologies of 9 May 1945 diaries.
add_eyes.bio: Samoilov was wounded in 1943 and returned to the front; he was decorated for the Berlin operation. His poems about his generation, which went straight from school to the war, became some of the best known in Russian. His diary entry for Victory Day is unusual for its doubt rather than its jubilation.

sources.title: Rossiyskaya Gazeta: 9 May 1945 in diaries and memoirs (Russian)
Snob: how Soviet writers and journalists remembered Victory Day (Russian)

add_eyes.name: Mikhail Prishvin
add_eyes.role: Writer and naturalist, aged 72, who kept a diary for nearly half a century
add_eyes.where: Moscow and the country outside it at Pushkino
add_eyes.vantage_label: elderly civilian far from the front
add_eyes.authenticity: Diaries kept from 1905 to 1954, much of them unpublishable in Soviet times and printed in full only from the 1990s. Not disputed.
add_eyes.bio: Prishvin's diary is a private counterweight to the official Victory: he records joy, but also his wife's anger at public celebration while so many were dead. He is the oldest voice in the chapter.

sources.title: Rossiyskaya Gazeta: 9 May 1945 in diaries and memoirs (Russian)

add_entries.headline: A historian starts recording the occupation for himself
add_entries.digest: Weeks after Warsaw surrendered, Ringelblum began collecting material on what was happening to the city's Jews, first as daily notes, later as weekly and monthly summaries. He wrote mainly in Yiddish, on loose sheets, as a historian's working notebook rather than a personal diary. Within a year the private chronicle had become the starting point for a collective underground archive.
add_entries.source_note: Holocaust Historical Society biography (his own statement that he began in October 1939); USHMM Oneg Shabbat article; JHI on vol. 29 of the complete edition

add_entries.date_display: Saturday 16 November 1940 and the days after
add_entries.headline: The ghetto gates close without warning
add_entries.digest: The sealing of the ghetto came as a shock; people had not believed it would happen. Ringelblum noted the mixed German, Polish and Jewish police posts at every crossing, Jewish women shut out of the market halls, food running out and prices jumping at once. In later notes he recorded that smuggling began from the first day, because official rations covered only a fraction of what people needed, and that smugglers, including small children, were shot.
add_entries.source_note: Ghetto closure date: IPN article; undated Ringelblum excerpt on the closure in 1943.pl 'Sealing of the Warsaw Ghetto' (PDF); smuggling note via Alpha History. Exact day of the note not given.

add_entries.date_display: Late June 1942 (BBC broadcast of Friday 26 June 1942)
add_entries.headline: The BBC broadcasts what the archive had gathered
add_entries.digest: On 26 June 1942 the BBC broadcast a report on the murder of Polish Jews, naming Słonim, Vilnius, Lwów and Chełmno, based on material from Bund activists and the Oyneg Shabes group that had been smuggled to London. Ringelblum noted that everything they knew had been told. The group felt for a moment that its work had reached the world and might bring help; less than four weeks later the mass deportations from Warsaw to Treblinka began.
add_entries.source_note: Jewish Historical Institute, 'June 26, 1942. BBC informs about the extermination of Polish Jews' (quoting Ringelblum's Chronicle of the Warsaw Ghetto, pp. 395–396); USHMM podcast page. Exact day of his note not stated.

add_entries.place: Basement of the Borochov school, 68 Nowolipki Street, Warsaw ghetto
add_entries.headline: Ten metal boxes buried under a school
add_entries.digest: Twelve days into the Great Deportation, on Ringelblum's orders, the teacher Israel Lichtensztajn and two former pupils, Dawid Graber (19) and Nachum Grzywacz (17), sealed the first part of the archive in ten metal boxes and buried them in the school cellar. The young men added their own testaments; Graber wrote that afternoon that they would be burying the last part in a moment, and that what they could not shout to the world they were hiding in the ground. Neither boy survived the deportations. The boxes were dug up on 18 September 1946.
add_entries.source_note: Jewish Historical Institute, 'Monday, August 3, 4 p.m. We'll be burying the last part in a moment'; USHMM Oneg Shabbat article; Mémorial de la Shoah Ringelblum exhibition

add_entries.headline: The second cache: two milk cans
add_entries.digest: With the ghetto reduced to a remnant after the deportations, the second part of the archive, including underground newspapers and calls to resistance, was packed into two large milk cans and buried in the same cellar. Lichtensztajn did the burying; only Ringelblum and two colleagues knew the place. That month Ringelblum and his family left for a hiding place on the 'Aryan side'. The cans were found by building workers on 1 December 1950.
add_entries.source_note: USHMM Oneg Shabbat article (Ringelblum and Lichtensztajn, February 1943); Mémorial de la Shoah exhibition ('end of February 1943'); JHI article on Lichtensztajn

add_entries.headline: A third cache, the day before the uprising
add_entries.digest: The last part of the archive was sealed in a metal cylinder and buried under a building at 34 Świętojerska Street, one day before the Warsaw ghetto uprising began. Ringelblum, who had slipped back into the ghetto, last saw Lichtensztajn on 17 April; the teacher died in the first days of the fighting with his wife and daughter. This third cache has never been found.
add_entries.source_note: USHMM Oneg Shabbat article (date and place); JHI article on Lichtensztajn (last meeting 17 April 1943)

add_entries.place: Stalingrad, with the 308th Rifle Division (Gurtiev) near the silicate works
add_entries.headline: Siberians hold the factory district, house by house
add_entries.digest: Grossman pieced together the 308th Division's month day by day from the men who survived it: the Germans reaching the silicate works on 2 October and taking it the next evening, a regiment cut down to eleven men, a tank crew out of shells throwing bricks. He noted an uneasy quiet on 12–13 October, a headquarters hit with heavy losses on the 14th, and two to three days of fighting from house to house after 17 October. He wrote it up for Red Star; to his wife he complained about the editors' meddling.
add_entries.source_note: A Writer at War, Stalingrad chapters, via HistoryNet excerpt ('Axis of the Main Attack' material and letter of 22 October 1942). Notes and article text are interleaved in the edition; exact days of writing not given.

add_entries.place: Site of Treblinka, east of Warsaw
add_entries.headline: At Treblinka, the camp the SS tried to erase
add_entries.digest: Soon after the Red Army reached the area, Grossman went to Treblinka, the camp to which most of the Warsaw ghetto's Jews had been sent in 1942. The SS had demolished it and planted it over, but he interviewed local peasants and surviving former prisoners and examined the ground. He wrote that it was the writer's duty to tell this terrible truth and the reader's civic duty to learn it. His essay appeared in Znamya in November 1944.
add_entries.source_note: Sources differ on the month: Goodenow-Weber substack (August 1944, publication November 1944), NLI blog and Undsoc (September 1944); duty phrase quoted in HistoryNet. Day unknown.

add_entries.headline: Victory in Berlin, and what the newspaper left out
add_entries.digest: In the last days of the battle and the first days of peace Grossman walked the ruined centre of Berlin. His published dispatches described celebration. His notebook also recorded Soviet soldiers who had drunk industrial chemicals from barrels in the Tiergarten, thinking it was alcohol, and died of it. The gap between the two shows how much he kept for himself.
add_entries.source_note: A Writer at War, ch. 27 'The Battle for Berlin' (April–May 1945; Connexions contents); Tiergarten notebook detail via The Critic, August 2026 review. Exact day not confirmed.

add_entries.headline: 'Beached at 0725': a padre lands under fire
add_entries.digest: Skinner's landing craft ran in at about seven in the morning and came under fire within minutes. He reached the beach at 0725, noting the time as precisely as the drill. Men beside him were hit, one losing a leg; he was thrown backwards onto a Bren carrier and got ashore unhurt except for a severe pain in his side. Then he began the work he would do all summer, tending the wounded and the dead.
add_entries.source_note: History News Network article on Skinner's D-Day diary (IWM holding)

add_entries.headline: From the sea: smoke, guns and thousands of barges
add_entries.digest: Raymond watched aircraft lay smoke between the fleet and the French coast while warships shelled the German batteries. He saw thousands of landing craft heading in and enemy shells falling around his own ship, and he wrote frankly about how frightened and tense the crew were. That night his flotilla engaged two German destroyers, which he recorded as sunk.
add_entries.source_note: Library of Virginia, Uncommonwealth blog on the Raymond diary (LVA Accession 50043). The sinking claim is his; post-war records may differ.

add_entries.headline: A day of joy and new doubts
add_entries.digest: Samoilov recorded Victory Day as a day of joy and, unexpectedly, of doubt. Until then the only question had been whether he would survive; now the question was how he would live. He also wrote down what he had heard of the surrender signing at Karlshorst the night before: Zhukov presiding, crowds of correspondents, and the German delegation leaving in silence.
add_entries.source_note: Rossiyskaya Gazeta, '9 May 1945 in diaries and memoirs' (2023); Snob article on Soviet writers' Victory Day, both citing Podyonnye zapisi

add_entries.date_display: Victory Day, 9 May 1945 (entry not exactly dated in the source)
add_entries.headline: An old writer and his wife argue over the celebrations
add_entries.digest: Prishvin drove his family out to Pushkino and thought about the living and the dead, and decided that victory was rightly a cause for joy. His wife Valeria was bitter at the public rejoicing and said people ought to be weeping. He argued that the dead would be remembered too, but admitted that he had himself felt the right to be sad when everyone else was happy.
add_entries.source_note: Rossiyskaya Gazeta, '9 May 1945 in diaries and memoirs' (2023), headed Victory Day; exact entry date not printed there

add_entries.headline: Two days after VE Day, a quiet declaration of independence
add_entries.digest: The surviving diary resumes just after the lost pages of 1944–45. Two days after VE Day Nella wrote that she loved her home as a home, not as a house to be kept, and that she would not go back to the way things were before the war, when her husband expected her to stay in and keep him company alone. The war had given her work and friendships she meant to keep.
add_entries.source_note: 'The diaries of Nella Last' (A Narrative of Their Own, Substack), quoting the entry of Thursday 10 May 1945. Entries for 3 September 1939 and 8 May 1945 could not be found: her diary begins later in September 1939, and pages from January 1944 to early May 1945 are lost (Wikipedia).

add_convergences.label: VE Day and Victory Day: the war in Europe ends
add_convergences.note: The surrender signed at Reims on 7 May and again at Karlshorst late on 8 May (already 9 May in Moscow) gives the end two dates. Lindgren sees Stockholm celebrate; Kellner refuses to excuse bystanders; Samoilov finds his relief turning into doubt about how to live; Prishvin's wife says people should weep; Grossman's notebook keeps the deaths his paper leaves out; Nella Last, two days on, resolves not to go back to her old life.

add_ties.note: Both were in Berlin as it fell in late April and early May 1945: Grossman with the Red Army, Hillers in a cellar among the women its soldiers assaulted. His notebooks are frank about the violence of Soviet troops in Germany.
Both ended the war with the Red Army in and around Berlin, one as a famous correspondent, the other as a young private who would become a poet.

Most of the Warsaw Jews whose lives Ringelblum's archive recorded were deported to Treblinka in summer 1942. Grossman walked the site of the camp two years later and wrote one of the first accounts of it.
Both documented the two largest ghettos in occupied Poland, Warsaw and Łódź, from the inside, and both left papers found only after the war.
On 6 June 1944 Skinner was going ashore at Gold Beach while Raymond's destroyer guarded the invasion fleet offshore: the same morning seen from the beach and from the sea.

updates.why: The Great Deportation from Warsaw began 22 July 1942 and the first Oyneg Shabes cache was buried 3 August 1942 (USHMM, JHI); new Ringelblum entry belongs in this cluster.
Added two eyewitness D-Day diaries (Skinner, Gold Beach, via HNN/IWM; Raymond, HMCS Saskatchewan, Library of Virginia Acc. 50043).

fix.authenticity: Written for the Mass Observation project from 1939 to 1966, about 12 million words in all, roughly 2 million of them from the war. Edited selection Nella Last's War (1981; reissued 2006). Her pages for January 1944 to the beginning of May 1945 were lost from the Mass Observation collection before it moved to Sussex University, so there is no D-Day or VE Day entry; the surviving record resumes days after VE Day. No entry for 3 September 1939 has been traced in published sources.

updates.why: Wikipedia confirms the lost span (Jan 1944 to beginning of May 1945); searches found no published 3 Sept 1939 or 8 May 1945 entry, while a 10 May 1945 entry is quoted.
